target_constraint: Must maintain screw preload under masticatory forces for 15+ years
observed_phenomenon: Implant-abutment screw loosening causing restoration failure
mechanism: Conical (Morse taper) implant-abutment connections provide higher removal force and better mechanical anchoring than external or internal hex connections, which can resist screw loosening under masticatory loads.
intervention: Replace the standard internal hex implant-abutment connection with a conical (Morse taper) connection design, and combine this with the existing torque-controlled tightening protocol to maintain screw preload over 15+ years.
expected_effect: The conical connection will increase the mechanical anchoring and removal force of the abutment, reducing the incidence of screw loosening and subsequent restoration failure under masticatory forces, thereby extending the functional lifespan of the implant system.
falsification_test: Conduct an in vitro cyclic loading test per ISO 14801:2015 comparing conical vs. internal hex connections (same implant diameter and bone level), measuring abutment removal force and screw loosening torque after 5 million cycles at 30° load; if the conical connection does not show significantly higher removal force and lower screw-loosening incidence than the internal hex, the intervention is falsified.
source_spans: "The highest removal force was recorded in conical (192.7 +/- 10.9 N) and internal hex (174.3 +/- 15.4 N) and the lowest were in the external hex (145.8 +/- 12.6 N). Important disparities between groups were identified (p < 0.05). Thus, the conical connections provide better mechanical anchoring, thus improving the stability of the implants."
